I've been farming this land in Quzhou for five decades. I know its rhythms better than I know my own pulse. At 72, farming alone on 6.5 mu, I have to be smart about labor — I can't afford to be on my knees pulling weeds for days. I rely on machinery where I can, and I use what works, not what's fashionable.

**Wheat (October planting):** I'll plant all 6.5 mu in the winter rotation. I use an improved variety — I've settled on a locally adapted line that handles our cold winters and gives steady 480-500 kg/mu. I won't chase new hybrids; the yield gains aren't worth the price and unfamiliarity at my age. I apply fertilizer in two splits — base phosphorus and potassium at plowing, then urea at jointing. Three irrigations: the pre-winter sealing water in November to protect roots, jointing in April, and grain filling in May. I spray twice: a herbicide pass in early spring before the weeds take hold, and a combined aphid-fungicide treatment at heading. Rotary tillage — I'm not ploughing deep every year anymore, my back can't take it and it's not necessary every cycle.

**Maize (June planting):** Straight into no-till after wheat harvest. I use hybrid seed — that's been standard here for thirty years and for good reason. Summer rain usually covers a lot of the water need, so I only pull from the well twice if it stays dry at jointing and tasseling. Nitrogen goes in twice: some compound fertilizer at planting, then a urea topdress at big bell stage. Two pesticide passes: herbicide right after emergence, then check for stem borer at bell stage. I expect around 600 kg/mu in a normal year.

This plan keeps my labor manageable, uses inputs I trust, and has fed me and my family for years.
